learningObjectives.title: Acids, bases and the pH scale

questions.q: Which ion do all acids produce when dissolved in water?
questions.explain: An acid is a substance that releases hydrogen ions (H+) in aqueous solution.

questions.q: What is the pH of a neutral solution such as pure water?
questions.explain: On the pH scale a neutral solution has a pH of exactly 7.

questions.q: Which ion is produced in solution by alkalis?
questions.explain: Alkalis dissolve in water to release hydroxide ions (OH-).

questions.q: What colour is universal indicator in a strongly acidic solution?
questions.explain: Universal indicator turns red in strongly acidic solutions (low pH).

questions.q: What colour is litmus in an alkaline solution?
questions.explain: Litmus is blue in alkalis and red in acids.

questions.q: What colour is phenolphthalein in an alkaline solution?
questions.explain: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali.

questions.q: A solution has a pH of 2. How is it best described?
questions.explain: A pH well below 7 (such as 2) indicates a strongly acidic solution.

questions.q: What is the definition of an alkali?
options: A substance that releases H+ ions
questions.explain: An alkali is a base that is soluble in water.

questions.q: What colour is methyl orange indicator in acidic solution?
questions.explain: Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkaline conditions.

questions.q: What are the general products when an acid reacts with an alkali?
options: A salt, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Neutralisation of an acid by an alkali produces a salt and water only.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents neutralisation?
questions.explain: In neutralisation, hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions to form water.

questions.q: What gas is produced when an acid reacts with a metal carbonate?
questions.explain: Acid + metal carbonate gives a salt, water and carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What gas is produced when a reactive metal reacts with an acid?
questions.explain: Acid + metal produces a salt and hydrogen gas.

questions.q: Which salts are formed when hydrochloric acid is neutralised?
questions.explain: Hydrochloric acid always produces chloride salts.

questions.q: Which salts are formed when sulfuric acid is neutralised?
questions.explain: Sulfuric acid always produces sulfate salts.

questions.q: Nitric acid is neutralised by potassium hydroxide. What salt is formed?
questions.explain: Nitric acid gives nitrate salts, so potassium hydroxide forms potassium nitrate.

questions.q: What are the products of the reaction between hydrochloric acid and magnesium oxide?
options: Magnesium chloride, water and carbon dioxide
questions.explain: Acid + metal oxide gives a salt and water; here magnesium chloride and water.

questions.q: Which process is used to obtain dry salt crystals from a salt solution?
questions.explain: The solution is evaporated to concentrate it, then left to crystallise, forming dry crystals.

questions.q: When making a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base, why is excess base added?
options: To ensure all the acid has reacted
questions.explain: Excess insoluble base guarantees all the acid is used up; the unreacted excess is then filtered off.

questions.q: How is the unreacted excess insoluble base removed after the salt solution has formed?
questions.explain: The excess solid base is separated from the salt solution by filtering.

questions.q: Which acid and insoluble base would you react to prepare copper(II) sulfate?
questions.explain: Sulfuric acid gives sulfates, and copper(II) oxide provides the copper, forming copper(II) sulfate and water.

questions.q: A soluble salt made from an acid and an alkali is best prepared using which technique?
options: Titration to find the exact volumes
questions.explain: As both reactants are soluble, titration is used to find the exact neutralising volumes so no excess remains.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Chemistry (2017) specification; Acids, Bases & Salts
